description_full: Douglas Emmett, Inc. is a fully integrated, self-administered and self-managed real estate investment trust , and one of the largest owners and operators of high-quality office and multifamily properties located in the premier coastal submarkets of Los Angeles and Honolulu. Douglas Emmett focuses on owning and acquiring a substantial share of top-tier office properties and premier multifamily communities in neighborhoods that possess significant supply constraints, high-end executive housing and key lifestyle amenities. Douglas Emmett, Inc. was incorporated in 1971 in Maryland and is based in Santa Monica, California.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 778 people. Revenue per employee of $1.3M ranks in the below the sector median among Real Estate peers. Each employee generates $250K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $27K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (10/10).
financial_summary: Douglas Emmett, Inc. is a mid-cap real estate business with a $2.0B market cap on $1.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +0% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 65% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $194M in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 23.78× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 13.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 1.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Management returns a meaningful 6.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 3.5% of the shares.

sect: The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 12% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 32% and a beta of 0.97, it moves roughly with the market.
About $19.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 46% in the 2020 crash, 57% in the 2022 bear market and 74% in 2008.
val: On multiples it looks cheap against Real Estate peers: P/FCF 10.5 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 9.5% (above the risk-free rate).
The 10 covering analysts target $12.40 on average, 22% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.54).
It runs a 65% gross margin and converts 19% of revenue into free cash flow.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 19%.
ROE of 1% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (4.9x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.1% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 13.1x net debt to EBITDA ($340.8M of cash against $5.5B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.7x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.09 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.3% over 3 years, 2.4% over 5 years and 4.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Free cash flow has compounded -6.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of -1.6% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (19.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 36.9% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.5%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only bought over the past year (3 purchases, net $1.5M bought).
It returns 6.2% a year to shareholders (7.5% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 844% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 28.7% of the float, 13.4 days to cover.
people: With about 778 employees, each generates about $1.3M of revenue, 0.6x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 3.8% a year.
That works out to $250K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $842K (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
